title: Twelve Scouts Explore Canaan
summary: At God's command Moses sends twelve tribal leaders from the Wilderness of Paran to explore Canaan. For forty days they travel from the southern desert to the far north, and they bring back a huge cluster of grapes from the Valley of Eshcol along with pomegranates and figs. They report that the land flows with milk and honey but that its people are strong and its cities fortified. Caleb urges the people to go up at once; the others spread a bad report that the land devours its inhabitants and that they felt like grasshoppers beside its giants.
story: Israel has reached the edge of the promise. More than a year after the exodus, the people are camped in the Wilderness of Paran near Kadesh, just south of Canaan. The land God swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lies ahead, and the scouts' task is to see it and bring back evidence. They find that everything God said about the land is true. What they cannot agree on is whether God can be trusted to give it. This chapter and the next form the turning point of Numbers. The complaints of chapters 11 and 12 were serious, but here the whole people will face a single decision, and its outcome will shape the next thirty-eight years. The scouts even visit Hebron, where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, and Jacob were buried, the one plot of Canaan Abraham had owned, and they stand at the graves of the promise without believing it.
historical:
The scouts cross the whole land, from the Wilderness of Zin in the south to Rehob near Lebo-hamath, a site often placed in the Beqaa Valley of modern Lebanon. The note that Hebron “had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt” (verse 22) refers to Tanis, a city in the eastern Nile delta; its precise reference point is debated, but the note stresses how ancient and established Hebron was. Kadesh, the base to which they return, is usually identified with the oasis region of Ain el-Qudeirat and Ain Qadeis in northeastern Sinai.

The peoples listed in verse 29 match the Bible's picture of Canaan: Amalekites in the southern Negev, Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites in the central hills, Canaanites along the coast and the Jordan. Archaeology has shown that many Canaanite cities of the second millennium BC were surrounded by massive walls and earthen ramparts, so the report of large fortified cities was not invented. Deuteronomy 1:22-23 adds that the people first proposed sending scouts and Moses approved; Numbers presents the mission as commanded by God. Many readers take the two as complementary, the people's request granted by God's permission.
cultural:
The scouts were sent in the season of the first ripe grapes (verse 20), which in the hill country falls in late summer. The cluster from the Valley of Eshcol, whose name means cluster, was so large that two men carried it on a pole, and the image has become a familiar symbol of the land's abundance. Milk and honey were the standard biblical description of a good land (Exodus 3:8): milk from flocks grazing rich pasture, and honey that may mean bees' honey or a thick syrup made from dates or other fruit. Both pointed to a land that could sustain herds and orchards, a sharp contrast to the desert where Israel was living on manna.

The descendants of Anak, with three named clans at Hebron, were remembered in Israel as a people of great height. The scouts' claim that they were Nephilim reaches back to Genesis 6:4, where the Nephilim are mighty men before the flood. Linking the Anakites to them made them sound like legendary giants, not ordinary enemies. In a world where kings boasted of their strength, the scouts' confession that they felt like grasshoppers says as much about their fear as about the enemy.
literary: The chapter moves from list to mission to debate. The twelve names (verses 4-15) echo the tribal lists of chapters 1 and 2, but these are different men, and only two of the names, Caleb and Hoshea, will matter. Moses' instructions (verses 17-20) are a string of paired questions: strong or weak, few or many, good or bad, camps or fortresses, fertile or poor. The report (verses 27-29) first answers well, then turns on a single word, nevertheless. Caleb's appeal (verse 30) is short and certain. The other scouts' reply grows darker as it goes, from “they are stronger than we are” to a land that “devours its inhabitants” to Nephilim, and ends with grasshoppers. The chapter ends mid-crisis with no response from the people, a cliffhanger resolved in chapter 14.

outline.t: Twelve leaders chosen; Hoshea renamed Joshua
Exploring the land; the cluster from Eshcol
The report: a good land with strong peoples
Caleb's call and the bad report of the others

doctrines.note: Caleb and the other scouts see the same land, the same fruit, and the same fortified cities. What differs is whether they trust God's promise. Faith in this chapter is not denying the size of the obstacles but weighing them against the one who promised.

The land is the land God swore to give Abraham's descendants, and the scouts confirm that it is everything he said. The promise is visible and tangible, carried back on a pole. The question is not whether God kept his word but whether his people will receive it.

The scouts' report moves from fact to exaggeration to slander, calling the good land a place that devours. Unbelief here is not quiet doubt; it spreads fear, rewrites God's gift as a threat, and draws the whole community with it.

words.note: Tur, to explore or search out. It is the chapter's key verb for the scouts' work. The same verb returns in 15:39, where the tassels on Israel's garments remind the people not to follow, or go exploring after, their own heart and eyes. The scouts' failure was not in looking but in trusting what their eyes told them over God's word.

Dibbah, a bad report, rumor, or slander. The word usually describes damaging talk spread about someone. Here the scouts spread it about the land itself (verse 32), and so, in effect, about the God who promised it. Their words, not only their fear, bring the disaster of chapter 14.

Nephil, the Nephilim. The word appears only here and in Genesis 6:4, and its meaning is debated; it may be related to the verb to fall. The scouts use it to turn the Anakites into legendary giants from before the flood, making the enemy seem beyond anyone's power to defeat.

Yehoshua, Joshua, meaning the LORD saves. Moses gives this name to Hoshea son of Nun (verse 16), whose original name meant salvation. The added element puts God's name into it. In Greek the name is Iesous, the same name given to Jesus.

christ: The scout whom Moses renamed Joshua, “the LORD saves,” bore the name that the angel later gave to Mary's son: “you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Joshua would one day lead Israel into the land, but Hebrews observes that he could not give the people final rest: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (Hebrews 4:8). The greater Joshua does. The fruit the scouts carried back also fits a New Testament pattern. It was a first taste of a land not yet possessed, and Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20) and says believers have “the firstfruits of the Spirit” (Romans 8:23), a real share now in what is still to come. These are thematic connections, drawn from the way the New Testament reads the wilderness story.

hard.q: If the Nephilim lived before the flood, how could the scouts have seen them in Canaan?
hard.a: Genesis 6:4 places the Nephilim before the flood, though it also says they were on the earth “and afterward as well,” which some take to mean after the flood too. Interpreters answer the question in several ways. Many point out that the claim comes from the scouts whose report the text calls bad (verse 32); they were exaggerating, using a legendary name to make the Anakites sound invincible, and the chapter does not endorse the claim. Others think Nephilim had become a general term for people of extraordinary size, not a claim of direct descent from the pre-flood figures. Those who read the flood as regional rather than worldwide have another option. Whichever answer is preferred, the chapter's own emphasis is plain: the report was shaped by fear, and Caleb, who saw the same people, later drove the sons of Anak out of Hebron (Joshua 15:14).

questions: Caleb and the others saw the same land and the same giants. What makes the difference between how they responded, and what shapes how you read the obstacles in front of you?
The scouts began with the facts and ended with exaggeration. How does fear change the way we describe our circumstances to others?
The scouts stood at Hebron, where the patriarchs were buried in the land God promised, and still doubted. What reminders of God's past faithfulness are close to you that you might overlook?
